conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for taking the time to speak with me today. I’m Dr. Ward, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS—with you. This is a brief, 10-question screening that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way for us to be sure we’re giving you the right support in these early weeks of motherhood.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety or the safety of someone else. We’ll go at your pace, and you can ask me to repeat or rephrase anything.

I’ll ask the questions conversationally—no paperwork on your end—then we’ll talk about what the results might mean and any next steps that could be helpful. Ready to begin?

Thinking about the past week, overall how have you been enjoying the things you used to take pleasure in—whether that’s music, food, a favorite show, or even small moments with your baby?

Honestly? Not much. I’ll put on the playlist I used to love, and it just feels...flat. Same with food—my sister brought over those lemon bars I used to devour, and I took two bites and felt done. Even when the baby gives me that little gummy smile, I’ll smile back, but the warm rush I expected isn’t really there. It’s like the volume got turned way down on everything I used to enjoy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I still laugh sometimes—like when my husband tripped over the diaper bag and did that little hop to keep from landing on the dog. But it fades fast, and I catch myself thinking, “I should feel happier about that,” instead of just enjoying it. Mostly, funny things feel kind of distant, like I’m watching them through a pane of glass.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about tomorrow—or next week—it’s mostly worry, not excitement. Like, I know I’m supposed to look forward to taking the baby to that “mommy-and-me” group on Thursday, but all I feel is dread that he’ll cry the whole time or I’ll forget something. Even simple stuff, like having coffee with a friend, feels like a chore I have to get through rather than something I used to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. Yesterday he spit up a ton right after I fed him and I kept thinking, “I must’ve over-fed him or held him wrong.” I know babies spit up, but I still felt like I messed up. When he wouldn’t nap, I kept replaying every little thing I did—was the room too bright, did I rock him too fast? I end up convinced it’s my fault when it probably isn’t.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly picture him choking in the bassinet, or I’ll hear an ambulance and imagine it’s because I missed some symptom. My heart races, I check his breathing four or five times a night, and I know it’s probably irrational, but I can’t help it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. It’s worst at night after I put him down. I’ll be brushing my teeth and suddenly feel this wave—like something awful is about to happen, tight chest, can’t catch my breath. No reason, just panic. I sit on the bathroom floor with the fan on so I don’t wake the baby while I try to breathe through it.
Things have been getting on top of me

They have. Some mornings I look at the sink full of bottles and the pile of laundry and feel like I’m drowning. I’ll start one chore, hear him cry, drop everything, then can’t figure out where I left off. I usually get the basics done—he’s always fed and changed—but by the end of the day I’m exhausted and still feel like I accomplished nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. I’ll finally get him down at 11, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain just spins—did I wash the paci that fell on the floor, am I doing enough “tummy time,” what if he rolls over in the night? I lie there for an hour or more, and sometimes wake up at 3 a.m. and can’t drift off again until five. It’s not every single night, but it’s been several this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket on me. I’ll watch the neighbors out the window with their stroller and feel like everyone else is lighter, happier. I cry a few times a week—usually when I’m alone folding onesies—and I just feel… empty and sad, even when there’s no clear trigger.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes. I’ll be rocking him in the nursery, everything quiet, and suddenly my eyes just start leaking. Yesterday it was because he wouldn’t latch right—nothing major—but I sat there with tears dripping on his blanket feeling like a failure. It happens three, maybe four times a week, and once I start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No. I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I never get to that place—I just want to feel like me again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

**Identified Symptoms/Concerns**  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, feelings of emptiness (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/interest in usually pleasant activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt/blaming self for minor infant issues (Q3)  
- Daily, intrusive anxiety/worry and nocturnal panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep disruption linked to racing thoughts/worry, beyond infant-care demands (Q7)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty completing tasks (Q6)  

**Pattern Summary**  
Consistent dysphoric mood, anhedonia, heightened anxiety/panic, and negative self-appraisal persisting “most days” and “several times a week.” Functional impairment reported in household tasks and social engagement.

**Safety**  
Denies self-harm ideation (Q10). No suicidal statements elicited.

**Screening Significance**  
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold and align with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum context. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment for postpartum depression and anxiety, plus safety planning given intensity of distress.
